newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Socialists threaten response to rallies.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialists threaten response to rallies.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists on Tuesday threatened a tougher response to opposition rallies, saying provincial party organisations had urged the party leadership to organise counter-rallies.

"They insist that we must have a tougher approach against the pressure of the opposition. Our local organisations also want to organise counter-rallies to respond to the opposition protest rallies," Vassil Karinov, a member of the party executive bureau, told reporters as daily protests entered their third week.
Counter-rallies by supporters of neighbouring Serbia's Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on December 24 led to clashes between demonstrators and police.

Student protesters gathered for a concert in front of the mausoleum which formerly housed the remains of Bulgarian Communist hero Georgi Dimitrov, and doctors protested outside the health ministry against their ill-equipped hospitals and falling living standards.
"It is absurd in Europe at the end of the 20th century to have patients bringing their own medicines and their own bandages to be treated in hospital," said one doctor.
The doctors said they planned daily protests until their demands for better pay and resources were met.
"I am happy because I am convinced victory is near. Victory will give young people a chance to believe in their future," said drama student Lili Bogdanova.
"We want not just to exist but to live. We want professional fulfilment and a chance to have normal families. If we have children, Bulgaria will have a future."

Karinov said the Socialists insisted on forming a new cabinet until general elections at the end of the year, and planned to introduce emergency economic measures in the next few weeks, including rescheduling the huge domestic debt.
"We think that immediate elections for Bulgaria are not the best alternative for the country because we need a tough restrictive regime even before a currency board system is introduced," he said.

Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov on Monday insisted that a new Socialist government was the only way to win new funding from international lenders, and proposed a "clean hands" operation to purge corrupt politicians.
The party on Tuesday elected Parvanov as chairman of the party's parliamentary group, replacing Krassimir Premyanov, who has attracted criticism for his business connections.

The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), which wants elections as soon as possible, said that if voting took place in March, a currency board fixed exchange rate regime could be introduced as early as May to stabilise the economy.

Both government and opposition have said they hope new president Petar Stoyanov, who takes office on Wednesday, can help break the deadlock over formation of a new government and scheduling of general elections.
Outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev has refused to ask the Socialists to form a new cabinet in the present atmosphere.
One-hour warning strikes took place in several factories and mines around the country. Miners are demanding higher wages to keep pace with annual inflation of more than 300 percent.

The Sofia civil prosecutor on Monday lifted a house arrest order against former Communist leader Todor Zhivkov on embezzlement charges but the military prosecutor's office said he remained under house arrest on a separate charge for his assimilation policy against ethnic Turks in the 1980s.
Stoyanov continued consultations on the crisis, meeting European Union ambassador Thomas O'Sullivan to discuss prospects for new funding.
Stoyanov, who said in his inaugural speech on Sunday he was keen to bring Bulgaria closer to Europe and NATO, will visit Brussels next week for talks with EU officials.
